notable_claims: Boston University asserted the right to conduct arbitrary searches of computer files without notice.
The BU policy is characterized as a violation of academic freedoms for faculty and students.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie critiques a Boston University policy that allows the administration to inspect data and files without notice. He argues that the policy establishes an 'administrative insecurity' rather than a technical one. Kadie asserts that such policies violate the academic freedoms of faculty and students.
classification.title: Re: Harrassment via email

notable_claims: Government ownership of property does not necessarily grant legal authority to search.
University policies may be formulated ex post facto to punish specific behaviors, as alleged in the NCSA case.
Academic rights regarding office privacy may exist independently of strict legal definitions.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the intersection of university resource usage, privacy rights, and disciplinary policies. The author argues that government ownership of computer systems does not automatically grant a right to search and critiques ex post facto policy creation in academic settings.
classification.title: Re: Harrassment via email

notable_claims: Under 18 USC ss 2511, electronic communication service providers may divulge inadvertently obtained communications to law enforcement if they pertain to a crime.
Providers may record the initiation or completion of communications to protect against fraudulent, unlawful, or abusive use of the service.
classification.summary: Aydin Edguer responds to an inquiry regarding the legality of service providers disclosing overheard criminal activity and monitoring lines. The response cites specific sections of the Electronic Communications Privacy Act (ECPA) of 1986 to explain legal exceptions for law enforcement reporting and fraud prevention. The post also directs readers to the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) for a copy of the ECPA.
classification.title: Re: Harrassment via email

notable_claims: The University of Illinois student code prohibits university officials from consenting to police searches of assigned offices without a warrant.
Custodial services are listed as an exception allowing entry into offices without notice.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie responds to a critique by Neil Rickert regarding the definition of privacy in academic spaces. Kadie cites the University of Illinois student code and a Joint Statement on Rights and Freedoms of Students to argue that university offices have specific privacy protections against searches.
classification.title: Harrassment via email

notable_claims: The OCF is dedicated to obtaining and managing open computing resources so that no campus member is denied the resources they seek.
The organization's spirit is traced back to the former Undergraduate Computing Facility.
Official OCF documents must be provided to interested parties without undue delay under a Freedom of Information clause.
classification.summary: This item provides the constitution of the Open Computing Facility (OCF) at UC Berkeley. The document outlines a democratic governance model for managing computer resources to ensure no member of the campus community is denied access. It includes a Bill of Rights covering nondiscrimination, privacy, and freedom of information.
classification.title: The OCF Constitution

notable_claims: The OCF democratically manages computer resources for thousands of users.
Board resolutions can be conducted via electronic voting.
classification.summary: The item provides the bylaws for Berkeley's Open Computing Facility (OCF), an organization dedicated to the democratic management of computer resources. The document outlines governance rules regarding board appointments, meeting frequency, and electronic voting procedures.

notable_claims: Disk quotas on email partitions can be perceived by users as implicit censorship.
Technical troubleshooting (e.g., using egrep for non-ASCII characters) is framed as distinct from 'reading' private mail.
organizations: University of Kentucky Engineering Computing Center
classification.summary: A system administrator outlines a tiered protocol for troubleshooting technical email issues while attempting to preserve user privacy on UNIX systems. The author discusses the ethical tension between administrative needs and privacy, specifically regarding the inspection of mailboxes and the implementation of disk quotas. He argues that disk quotas are a resource management necessity rather than a form of censorship.
classification.title: Email privacy vs. System management

notable_claims: System administrators should not intervene in irresponsible user behavior regarding disk space usage.
Resource allocation issues are best solved via departmental billing or increasing hardware capacity.
classification.summary: Joe Buck responds to Sanjay Kapur regarding the tension between system administration and user behavior concerning disk quotas. Buck argues that administrators should not micromanage irresponsible users and suggests that resource shortages be solved through departmental billing or purchasing more hardware.
classification.title: Re: Email privacy vs. System management

notable_claims: CAF discussions were gatewayed to alt.comp.acad-freedom.talk and alt.comp.acad-freedom.news
classification.summary: Carl Kadie announces that Computers and Academic Freedom mailing lists have been made available as Usenet newsgroups. He provides instructions for users to migrate from the mailing lists to these new groups or to unsubscribe via listserv. The announcement details two specific newsgroups: one for general discussion and one moderated version for curated notes.
